extracted.intended_audience: young/entry-level newspaper reporters; journalism students; cub reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical textbook guidance for entry-level newspaper reporters on finding, evaluating, and writing news across beats (city, police, courts, speeches, meetings, weather, sports, society, etc.). Emphasizes professional ethics, accuracy, and techniques for making stories readable and newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests for news values; instincts as a source of reader-interest; distinction between 'interest' and 'importance'; timeliness; traditions; cycles and waves (e.g., crime waves, sensationalism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reader-identification, timeliness, and tests described in book to judge newsworthiness. Local news generally has more value than distant glamour; instincts and quick changes in values must be observed. (See chapters on News Values and index entries: tests for news values, interest vs importance, timeliness, traditions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard news-story structure (Five W's)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard news-story structure built around the Five W's (who, what, when, where, why) with a lead that supplies identification and primary facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads should place the five W's appropriately; the body should elaborate in descending importance. Different story types (accident, speech, court, interview) adapt the standard structure (see chapters 'News Story Structure', 'Five W's').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead writing (types and economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads may be combination, periodic, participial, paraphrase, slogan, or figure-based; avoid overcrowded first sentence; leads must be crafted for the story type (speech lead, accident lead, sports lead, sectional story lead).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match lead type to story (e.g., speech leads 100-107, accident leads 274-280). Keep leads clear, avoid stuffing too many facts into one sentence, and elaborate the lead properly in the body.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy / Precision
rubrics_metrics.description: Constant demand for exactness of both fact and statement; no circumlocutions allowed in reporting — exact temperatures, names, dates, and locations required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check facts with sources; copy desk and proof room inspect for errors. 'Accuracy Always' is enforced in style sheets. Even small errors (e.g., wrong street or initial) produce reader complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectivity / Avoid editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Report what was done and said; leave judgment to readers rather than using the reporter's opinions or charged adjectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid phrases that interpret or judge (e.g., 'far-fetched speech'); present evidence and quotations so readers can decide. Separate news page from editorial page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Currency of information (timeliness) is a core element of news values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize fresh, time-sensitive information; cycles and speed of change influence what gets covered and how it's presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local or 'home-grown' news preference
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinarily the most interesting news is that about the newspaper's own readers; local items often outrank distant glamorous items in reader interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give ample space to local reporting; cultivate beats that cover the front yard of readers (examples: Johnsons' golden wedding, local kitchen fire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat reporting and specialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters are assigned to beats or 'runs' (city hall, police, courts, business, church) and become the paper's specialist on those topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain regular contact with sources on the beat; specialization builds authority and career value. Best beats go to competent and reliable reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning the city / local knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter must study and know city geography, institutions, neighborhoods, local history, and where information congregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time learning the places and sources that produce news (Chamber of Commerce, unions, historical society, etc.). This knowledge aids verification and story ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional attitude and continual learning
rubrics_metrics.description: View reporting as a profession: be a student who never stops learning and investigating; develop expertise in subjects encountered on the beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend training, study subjects (e.g., fire alarms) sufficiently to be an 'authority' to readers and editors. Professionalism leads to better work and promotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics of news gathering (methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must be enterprising and persistent but 'gentlemen' — avoid illegal/unethical methods such as keyhole snooping, masquerading, theft, or other banditries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: City editors expect ethical conduct; past tabloid ruffianism declined as educational standards and public response increased. Methods that risk public trust are forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-the-record handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Tests for off-the-record matter; keeping confidences; salvaging and quoting officials; handling unprintable material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the book's tests to decide whether off-the-record material can be used; learn techniques for salvaging stories and when to honor confidences (see chapter 'Off the Record').

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel law and legal responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand libel definitions, defenses (truth, fair comment, privilege), civil vs criminal libel, and the responsibility of newspaper for statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn local libel rules, what public officials' utterances entail, the importance of truth, and conditions of privilege; be cautious in court and police reporting to avoid libel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of government records as primary sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Government offices are zealous information-collecting agencies; newspapers borrow heavily from public records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tap municipal, county, state, and federal records regularly; learn to read and explain their forms. Regular reporters on these offices build trust and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source types and verification (executives, social contacts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sources (executives, social contacts, curators, unions) supply different kinds of tips and facts; verification is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify tips at the authoritative repository (e.g., Chamber of Commerce for conventions). Don't let sources dictate copy; corroborate before publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviewing skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing includes preparation (questions), listening, note-taking, handling hostile or unresponsive interviewees, follow interviews, and the symposium interview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes, prepare but be flexible, manage stage fright and one-word answers, use follow-ups, and structure interview stories (see chapters 'Interviewing' and 'Interview Forms').

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech coverage techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Covering speeches involves note-taking/shorthand, identifying the speech's elements (lead-matter, subject, title), paraphrase vs direct quotes, and condensing speeches for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate lead forms for speeches, paraphrase when necessary, include speaker identification, correct speaker grammar when needed, and use abstracts/advance copies when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meetings coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting stories require verifying programs, selecting human-interest angles, analyzing reports of officers, and avoiding common faults in meeting copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify readers, check programs, use human-interest material to enliven routine reports, and structure meeting stories to highlight important outcomes first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime reporting ethics and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime news requires accuracy, inclusiveness, proper relation with police, care in giving details, explaining reasons for arrest, and ethics regarding suspects and 'alleged' labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drawing unwarranted inferences, be careful with charges and 'alleged', keep stories alive without sensationalism, and follow office policies to prevent libel or prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Accident news must capture witness statements, chronology, witness credibility, 'with' stories, and structure tailored to the accident lead and details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect accurate witness quotes, avoid gratuitous gore, use roundups for multiple accidents, and construct leads and body to cover who, what, when, where, how.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Court news requires knowledge of trial procedure, jury selection, indictments, habeas corpus, objections, testimony writing, and avoidance of libelous assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the law basics, record testimony accurately, understand court terminology and procedures, and structure court stories so readers understand legal steps and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obituary writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Obituaries require accuracy, advance obituary preparation, careful diction, limits on adjectives, tributes, attention to dangers (e.g., 'black sheep'), and news identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain morgue files, prepare advance obits, verify facts with hospitals/families, avoid excessive praise that misleads, and structure obituaries for reader interest and sensitivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports news demands accuracy in scores and facts, appropriate diction (avoid excessive slang), box scores, leads customized for sports, running stories, and ethical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep accurate statistics, craft leads that reflect game significance, manage speculation, and be mindful of radio influence and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weather reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather stories need essential information from authoritative sources, use of statistics, leads appropriate to freaks or regular forecasts, and options like ruled inserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accurate meteorological data, avoid superlatives, choose whether to run one long story or several short pieces, and employ statistics to support narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style sheet and office preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Every office issues a style sheet detailing preferences and prohibitions; it frames 'Accuracy Always' and stylistic conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and follow the office style sheet; understand house rules for consistent copy and to avoid surprises at the copy desk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copy editing and proofreading
rubrics_metrics.description: Copy desk inspects facts and language; proof room corrects typesetting errors; headline and run corrections may stop a print run.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mark copy correctly, respond to copy desk queries, expect rigorous checking, and accept revisions as part of producing publishable copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story variations and feature writing (color stories, sectional stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature, color, and sectional stories have distinct structures and lead variants (e.g., human-interest leads, inserts, ruled insert), and are used to brighten coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use color stories to create reader identification and interest; develop features using narrative techniques while obeying accuracy and relevance to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of direct and indirect quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotes carry individuality; indirect quotation/paraphrase is used to condense and clarify speeches/interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance direct and indirect quotes to preserve speaker voice while keeping copy concise and accurate; follow guidance in speech and interview chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length and sentence variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Vary sentence openings and lengths; use periodic and periodic-like sentences and paragraph length to change pace and readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid monotony and overly long paragraphs; use sentence variety to direct reader attention and sustain rhythm (see 'sentence variety' and 'paragraph length').

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-interest and 'color' material
rubrics_metrics.description: Brighten stories with human-interest material and color detail without sacrificing accuracy or taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find anecdote, local personality, or sensory detail that identifies readers with the story; avoid sensational or grotesque detail that repels readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites, folio stories and follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems for rewrites and folio (folo) stories, tie-ins with first-day pieces, and varieties of follow-up stories are essential for continuous coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rewrites to refine narrative and add new facts; plan folos to keep stories current; tie folo material to earlier coverage for continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive stories and scoops
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue exclusives and scoops that give the paper competitive advantage; exclusives require verification and protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate sources, guard leads, and verify facts before publishing; balance speed with accuracy to preserve credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicity writing and propaganda distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity writing (campaigns, propaganda forms) must be organized and planned; reporters who do publicity must know when it's allowable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep publicity efforts separate from news reporting; when a reporter writes publicity, plan campaigns carefully and disclose roles to avoid conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and 'making your own luck'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should transmute enthusiasm into work that gains executive notice; find unexploited beats and add sparkle to routine items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for opportunities (e.g., neglected beats like railroads) and develop specialty knowledge that raises your value to the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of sensationalism and management of graphic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphic and sensational detail can provoke reader protest and loss of patronage; newspapers must moderate use of horrifying details even if they 'work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heed public reaction (e.g., 'And Sudden Death' example); avoid gratuitous gore; use restraint to maintain readers and community standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting vs criticism (arts coverage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate reporting on theater/music from criticism; reporting should inform, criticism may evaluate but belongs on editorial/crit pages or clearly labeled columns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report objectively on events while reserving critical judgment to proper outlets; be tolerant and avoid mixing unmarked critique into news copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in political and labor reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Political and labor news require specific devices to obtain fairness; avoid cynicism and overemphasis of racial aspects or partisan spin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn the field, employ devices for balance (quotes from opposing sides), and be mindful of libel risks when covering candidates or unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the 'morgue' / reference library
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a newspaper morgue (reference library) for past obituaries and background material to support accuracy and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the morgue to prepare advance obituaries, backgrounders, and to verify historical facts; keep it organized for rapid retrieval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of figures and statistics in leads and copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures can be effective lead material; use accurate statistics and numbers to support news points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check numerical facts carefully; use figures to clarify significance but avoid cluttering the lead with too many numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader-identification and psychology (making stories inviting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present stories to meet reader psychology so they will be eagerly read; newspaper readers skim rather than study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make stories inviting with engaging leads, local angles, clear structure, and readable prose to suit skimming behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program and source verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify event programs, speakers, claims, and other source-provided details before filing copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check programs, dates, and claims with organizers or authoritative repositories; avoid reporting based on unverified tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling interviewees who won't talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics and tactics for dealing with interviewees who refuse to speak; salvaging material without misrepresenting their stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect refusals, seek alternative sources, use background/context, and avoid implying statements were made when they weren't.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking copy and make-up conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark stories that carry, indicate cuts, use ruled inserts for weather, and follow page make-up instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn newsroom marking conventions (cuts, ruled insert); mark copy clearly for the make-up editor to save time and avoid errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working under deadline and speed
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must produce accurate copy quickly (example: 'You've got twelve minutes, Harry; give me a quarter-column'), balancing speed with reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice rapid interviewing and concise writing; rely on verification habits and the copy desk safety net to meet short deadlines without sacrificing core accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorthand/note-taking for speeches and interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Use shorthand and effective note-taking methods when covering speeches and interviews to capture key phrases and structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take notes on trademark phrasings, chronology, and key quotes; notes enable accurate condensation and proper quotation in the lead and body.
